draft.title: Trust / credibility signals (Fogg / Stanford)
draft.principle_summary: Fogg's Stanford Web Credibility research (Stanford-Makovsky 2002 study, n greater than 4500, distilled into the Stanford Guidelines for Web Credibility, plus the earlier Fogg et al. 2001 CHI paper What Makes Web Sites Credible, n=1400) found credibility is judged as a combination of perceived TRUSTWORTHINESS (honest, unbiased) and EXPERTISE (knowledgeable, competent), and that the average visitor judges this mostly from fast, superficial visual cues (46.1% of subjects cited overall visual design as a credibility factor) rather than deep content evaluation. Of the 10 published guidelines, the ones with a direct Solen surface application are: (1) make information easy to verify (cite sources, show references), (2) show a real organization stands behind the site (legal name, address, real photos of real people and places, not stock), (3) highlight expertise and credentials of the people or providers, (5) make contact information easy to find, (6) professional visual design matched to purpose, (9) use restraint with promotional content so ads or offers do not read as noise that undercuts trust, (10) avoid errors of any size (typos, broken links, layout glitches) since a single visible defect drops perceived credibility disproportionately. This is a design-canon-level PERCEPTUAL framework, distinct from the honesty and no-fabrication ethics lines already enforced in PSYCHOLOGY.md: Fogg is about what visual and structural cues cause a user to believe a source is trustworthy, not about whether the underlying claim is true.

sources.claim: 46.1 percent of surveyed users judged web credibility in part on the appeal of overall visual design (layout, typography, font size, color scheme).

draft.proposed_addition:
## Domain: Credibility signals (Fogg / Stanford Web Credibility)

DECISION: any element whose job is to make the user trust the salon/provider/platform (badges, verified markers, provider photos, credential lines, contact info, review counts) is graded against the Fogg trustworthiness plus expertise framework before it ships, and a maximum of one credibility marker of each TYPE appears per card so markers read as signal, not decoration.

FORCES: showing more trust markers feels like it should increase trust, but Fogg's own guideline 9 (restraint with promotional content) and the observed Baymard finding that visual glitches near a trust-sensitive moment make users suspect a breach both point the other way: markers stacked past a small number read as compensating for something, and any marker that cannot be substantiated (an unverified "Verified" badge, a stock photo standing in for the real salon) is worse than no marker, because Fogg's guideline 10 (avoid errors of any size) treats a caught fake credibility cue as a credibility-destroying error, not a neutral omission.

OPTIMIZES FOR: the visitor's fast, largely visual first-pass judgment of trustworthiness and expertise (Fogg and Tseng 1999, T2) landing correctly within the sub-second window PSYCHOLOGY.md's 100ms trust window law already names, using cues Solen can actually back with real data: real self-hosted salon/staff photography (ties to PSYCHOLOGY.md's photos-first law, cross-reference, do not duplicate), a real review count next to any star (PSYCHOLOGY.md law 6, already gated), and, where the underlying fact exists, a provider credential or years-active line.

SACRIFICES: a verified-salon or verified-provider badge is explicitly NOT proposed here as a shippable UI element. Solen currently has no verification process or backing data field for it (confirmed by grep: zero components implement a trust-verification badge), so per the no-fabricated-data taste rule this stays a documented mechanic with no visual instantiation until an owner decision creates the underlying verification pipeline. Shipping a badge ahead of the data would itself be the Fogg guideline-10 violation this domain exists to prevent.

BOUNDARY: this domain governs PERCEPTUAL credibility cues (what makes a real thing look trustworthy). It does not govern factual honesty (that is PSYCHOLOGY.md's ethics bar, unchanged) and it does not reopen or restate the checkout-specific Baymard payment-field material in TASTE_CHECKOUT.md lines 10-13, which stays the canonical source for payment-form trust and is cross-referenced, not duplicated, here. It also does not relitigate the frozen salon-card badge copy or placement locked at RATIONALE.md:530-534; it only supplies the sourced boundary condition (Fogg guideline 9 restraint) that DECISION was missing.

MECHANIC: Fogg and Tseng 1999 (CHI 99, T2) frame credibility as trustworthiness times expertise, both perceptual, both judged fast; the Stanford-Makovsky 2002 study (T2, n greater than 4500) found 46.1 percent of subjects cited overall visual design as a credibility factor, meaning polish is doing real credibility work, not just aesthetic work, and this is the same aesthetic-usability mechanic RATIONALE.md line 179 already cites for perceived usability, extended here to perceived trust. The Stanford Guidelines for Web Credibility (2002, T2, credibility.stanford.edu/guidelines) give the 10-item checklist; the Solen-relevant subset is guideline 2 (real organization, real photos), guideline 3 (highlight real expertise/credentials), guideline 5 (findable contact info), guideline 9 (restraint with promotional content, i.e. the one-marker-per-type cap proposed above), and guideline 10 (a caught error or fake cue is disproportionately damaging). Taste-Lab probe to calibrate the one-marker-per-type cap on a real Solen salon card: show three variants of the same card (zero markers, one marker, three-plus stacked markers) to a small owner/pilot-salon panel and ask which reads as most trustworthy versus most like an ad; if three-plus wins, the restraint reading of guideline 9 needs re-weighting against Solen's specific market before the cap is written into RATIONALE as a hard number.

SOURCE: credibility.stanford.edu/guidelines (Fogg 2002, Stanford Guidelines for Web Credibility, T2); credibility.stanford.edu/pdf/p80-fogg.pdf (Fogg and Tseng 1999, The Elements of Computer Credibility, CHI 99, T2); credibility.stanford.edu/pdf/Stanford-MakovskyWebCredStudy2002-prelim.pdf (Stanford-Makovsky Web Credibility Study 2002, T2); cross-reference PSYCHOLOGY.md law 5 price-transparency, law 6 stars-never-bare, law 9 real-numbers-only, and the 100ms trust window law (do not duplicate); cross-reference _design-system/research/TASTE_CHECKOUT.md lines 10-13 for the Baymard payment-field-specific perceived-security material (T2, already sourced, do not duplicate); cross-reference RATIONALE.md line 179 aesthetic-usability effect (T2) as the adjacent mechanic this domain extends from perceived usability to perceived trust.
draft.taste_lab_probe: Three-variant salon-card panel test: same salon, same photo, zero trust markers vs one marker (real review count) vs three-plus stacked markers (badge + verified tag + credential line). Ask a small owner/pilot-salon panel which card they would trust most and which feels most like an advertisement. Result calibrates whether the proposed one-marker-per-type restraint cap (Fogg guideline 9) should become a hard number in RATIONALE or needs loosening for Solen's specific market before it is locked.

claim_verdicts.claim: Fogg and the Stanford Persuasive Technology Lab published the Stanford Guidelines for Web Credibility (2002), a 10-guideline distillation of a three-year research program surveying over 4,500 people.
claim_verdicts.note: Confirmed via credibility.stanford.edu/guidelines and multiple secondary sources: the Guidelines page describes the underlying program as three years of research including over 4,500 people, and lists exactly 10 numbered guidelines matching the draft's subset (guideline 2 real organization, 3 expertise, 5 contact info, 9 promotional restraint, 10 avoid errors). The 4,500 figure belongs to the cumulative multi-year program, not a single study, which is where the next claim goes wrong.

claim_verdicts.claim: 46.1 percent of surveyed users judged web credibility in part on the appeal of overall visual design.
claim_verdicts.note: Confirmed. Fogg et al. 2003 (ACM DUX) reports design look mentioned in 46.1 percent of participant comments, in the Stanford-Makovsky 2002 study of 2,684 people. CORRECTION: the draft mislabels this study's own n as greater than 4500. Actual n is 2,684; the 4,500-plus figure is the cumulative multi-study Persuasive Technology Lab research base, a different number describing a different thing. Fixed in verified_addition.

claim_verdicts.claim: Credibility on the web resolves into perceived trustworthiness and perceived expertise.
claim_verdicts.note: Confirmed. Fogg and Tseng 1999 (CHI 99) is the conceptual-framework paper defining this two-component model; it is not itself the empirical n=1400 study (that is the separate Fogg et al. 2001 CHI paper). Draft's citation is accurate as a conceptual reference and correctly kept separate from the n=1400 line.

claim_verdicts.claim: Payment fields need visual encapsulation to read as secure; trust badges 1-2 max inside the block; security concern concentrates at the card-number field.
claim_verdicts.note: Baymard Institute is a real, verifiable UX research firm and the general direction is corroborated by secondary sources. Already cited and tiered in TASTE_CHECKOUT.md lines 10-13; cross-referenced here per the draft's own scoping, not re-verified line by line.

claim_verdicts.claim: 19 percent of 2025 checkout abandonment was explicit card-data distrust (n=1026).
claim_verdicts.note: Already sourced and tiered in TASTE_CHECKOUT.md; cross-referenced only, not independently re-verified per the do-not-duplicate instruction.

verified.residual_risks: One factual correction was made and must be carried into the shipped doc: the draft conflated the Stanford Persuasive Technology Lab's cumulative three-year research base (over 4,500 people, spread across many studies, per the Guidelines page itself) with the n of the single Stanford-Makovsky 2002 study that produced the 46.1 percent visual-design finding (that study's actual n is 2,684). The corrected SOURCE section separates these two numbers; if the shipped RATIONALE entry states a bare number without this distinction it will re-introduce the error. Two things stay owner-decision, not verifier calls: (1) the one-marker-per-type cap is proposed but explicitly unlocked pending the taste-lab panel probe named in the draft, do not write it into RATIONALE as a hard number until that panel runs; (2) whether Solen ever builds a real salon/provider verification pipeline is an open product question this domain deliberately does not answer, it only pre-commits that if such a badge ships, it must be backed by real verification data, never decorative. Neither is a QUESTIONS.md candidate that fights a locked literal; both are new-domain calibration steps the draft itself already flagged.
